title: Statistical Treatment of Data (With Examples) | AnswerThis
summary: Learn how to write the statistical treatment of data in Chapter 3: match questions to statistics, use each formula and interpret a weighted mean.
body_markdown:
The statistical treatment of data is the part of Chapter 3 that names each statistic you will use, the research question it answers and how you will interpret the result. It shows your panel that every question in your study has a matching analysis.


Students in the Philippines usually write this section near the end of Chapter 3. This guide shows how to match each research question to a statistic, gives the formula for each common tool and walks through a weighted mean example by hand. It ends with sample paragraphs you can adapt.


## The statistical treatment of data: what it is and where it goes


Your statement of the problem lists the questions your study must answer. The statistical treatment of data tells the reader how you will answer each one with numbers.


A complete section does three things for every research question:


-


It names the statistic, such as a weighted mean or a t-test.


-


It says why that statistic fits the question and the data.


-


It explains how you will read the result, such as an interpretation scale or a significance level.


Schools name and place this section differently. Some end Chapter 3 with a heading called Treatment of Data. Others call it Statistical Treatment or Data Analysis. Follow your school’s manual.


## Matching each research question to a statistic


Start from your research questions, not from a list of tests. Most questions in a Philippine thesis fall into four types.


Type of question


Example question


Statistic to use


Profile


What is the profile of the respondents in terms of age, sex and year level?


Frequency and percentage


Level or extent


What is the level of study habits of the respondents?


Weighted mean (for Likert scale items), with standard deviation


Relationship


Is there a significant relationship between study habits and academic performance?


Pearson r for two numeric variables, or chi-square for two categorical variables


Difference


Is there a significant difference in study habits between male and female respondents?


t-test for two groups, or one-way ANOVA for three or more groups

## Common statistical tools, with formulas


Each tool below lists its formula, what it tells you and when to use it. Check every formula against your statistics textbook or your adviser’s notes before you put it in your paper.


### Frequency and percentage


P = (f ÷ N) × 100, where f is the number of respondents in a category, and N is the total number of respondents.


Use it to describe categories, such as sex, year level or school type. It answers profile questions.


### Weighted mean


WM = Σfx ÷ N, where f is the number of respondents who chose a scale point, x is the value of that point, and N is the total number of respondents.


Use it to find the average response to a Likert scale item or set of items. It answers level or extent questions. A worked example appears in the next section.


### Standard deviation


s = √\[Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1)\], where x̄ is the sample mean, and n is the sample size.


Use it with a mean to show how spread out the responses are. A small value means the respondents answered in a similar way.


### Pearson r


r = Σ\[(x − x̄)(y − ȳ)\] ÷ √\[Σ(x − x̄)² × Σ(y − ȳ)²\]


Use it to measure the direction and strength of a straight-line relationship between two numeric variables. The value runs from −1 to +1. A value near 0 means no straight-line relationship.


### t-test for two independent groups


t = (x̄₁ − x̄₂) ÷ √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂)


Use it to compare the means of two groups, such as male and female respondents. This is the form for unequal variances. The[two-sample t-test](https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/eda/section3/eda353.htm) also gives the pooled form for equal variances.


### One-way ANOVA


F = MS between groups ÷ MS within groups, where MS is a mean square, a sum of squares divided by its degrees of freedom.


Use it to compare the means of three or more groups, such as year levels. A significant F tells you that at least one mean differs. A post hoc test then shows which ones.


### Chi-square test of independence


χ² = Σ\[(O − E)² ÷ E\], where O is the observed count in a cell and E is the count you would expect if the two variables were unrelated.


Use it to[test](https://openstax.org/books/statistics/pages/11-3-test-of-independence) whether two categorical variables are related, such as sex and preferred learning mode.

A weighted mean of 3.98 falls between 3.41 and 4.20, so the respondents agree with the statement. Some schools use other labels, such as “often” or “highly evident”. Put the scale you use in your paper, so readers can check your interpretation.


*From frequencies to a verbal interpretation: the weighted mean of 3.98 falls in the agree band of the scale.*


## Statistical treatment of data examples


The three short examples below show how the section changes with the design. Adapt the wording to your own questions and scale.


### A descriptive study


“Frequency and percentage were used to describe the profile of the respondents. The weighted mean and standard deviation were used to determine the level of study habits. Each weighted mean was interpreted using the five-point scale in Table 3.”


### A correlational study


“Pearson r was used to determine the relationship between study habits and academic performance. The relationship was tested at the 0.05 level of significance. A positive r means that higher scores in study habits go with higher grades.”


### A comparative study


“An independent samples t-test was used to compare the study habits of male and female respondents. One-way ANOVA was used to compare the study habits of the four year levels. Where ANOVA showed a significant difference, a post hoc test identified which groups differed.”


## How to write the statistical treatment of data


Follow these five steps to write the section.


### 1. List your research questions in order


Copy each question from your statement of the problem. Write the section in the same order, so readers can match each question to its analysis.


### 2. Name one statistic for each question


Use the matching table above. Name only the statistics you will actually use.


### 3. Say why each statistic fits


Give one sentence on the data it needs, such as two groups or two numeric variables. If your instrument uses a scale, our guide to the[research instrument](https://answerthis.io/blog/research-instrument) explains how to report its reliability with Cronbach’s alpha.


### 4. Give your interpretation rules


Include the interpretation scale for weighted means and the significance level for tests. Many studies use 0.05, but state the level you chose.


Plan to report an effect size along with each p-value. Note that a[p-value](https://doi.org/10.1080/00031305.2016.1154108) does not measure the size of an effect or the importance of a result.


### 5. Name your tools


Say which software or calculator you used. The AnswerThis[research calculators](https://answerthis.io/research-calculators) are free, unlimited and run in your browser. They turn a test statistic into a p-value, turn summary numbers into confidence intervals and effect sizes, and compute Cronbach’s alpha, ICC and Cohen’s kappa from an item or rating table. They do not run a t-test, ANOVA or chi-square test on raw data, and they do not compute a weighted mean, so use a spreadsheet or a statistics package for those.


For effect sizes, the AnswerThis[effect size calculator](https://answerthis.io/effect-size-calculator) gives Cohen’s d, Hedges’ g, odds ratios and Pearson r. It shows confidence intervals for odds ratios and r, but not for d or g.


To run the analysis itself on your own data, follow our tutorial on how to[analyse data](https://answerthis.io/guide/steps-to-analyse-data-using-answerthis) in AnswerThis. It runs the tests you ask for, reports the results in words and saves a chart. For more on how the statistics fit the rest of your methods, see our[research methodology examples](https://answerthis.io/blog/research-methodology-examples-practical-guide) .


## Common mistakes


-


Listing tests you never run. Every statistic in this section should appear again in Chapter 4.


-


Leaving out the interpretation scale. Without it, readers cannot check what 3.98 means.


-


Using a t-test for three or more groups. Running several t-tests raises the chance of a[false positive](https://answerthis.io/blog/type-1-and-type-2-errors) , so use ANOVA instead.


-


Treating a p-value as the size of an effect. A small p-value can come with a tiny difference.


-


Using Pearson r for categories. For two categorical variables, use chi-square.


## Conclusion


A strong statistical treatment of data reads like a plan your panel can check line by line. Each research question gets one statistic, a reason and a rule for reading the result. Write it before you collect data, and you will know exactly what to run and report in Chapter 4. Those results then lead to the[recommendations](https://answerthis.io/blog/recommendation-in-research) you write in Chapter 5.


## FAQs


### What is the statistical treatment of data in research?


It is the part of the methodology chapter that names the statistics you will use, the question each one answers and how you will interpret the results.


### What is the weighted mean formula?


WM = Σfx ÷ N. Multiply each scale value by the number of respondents who chose it, add the products and divide by the total number of respondents.


### Which statistical tool should I use for a Likert scale?


Use the weighted mean to describe the level of agreement, with the standard deviation for spread. To compare groups or test relationships, use the test that fits your question and data.


### What is the difference between a t-test and ANOVA?


A t-test compares the means of two groups. One-way ANOVA compares the means of three or more groups in one test.


### Where does the statistical treatment of data go in a thesis?


It usually comes at the end of Chapter 3, after the data gathering procedure. Some schools call it Treatment of Data or Data Analysis, so check your thesis manual.
